Pedestrians walk next to a screen showing the commodity futures for crude oil in the Jing'an district of Shanghai on Monday.Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesIn less than two months, United States President Donald Trump has taken out two of Beijing’s closest allies — threateningChina’s oil supply in the process.Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the US in January. A US KC-135 Stratotanker, a refueling aircraft, went down in western Iraq on Thursday, the US military said, though the incident was “not due to hostile fire or friendly fire.”  The statement did not specify whether any US service members were hurt or killed.“The incident occurred in friendly airspace during Operation Epic Fury, and rescue efforts are ongoing,”a releasefrom US Central Command said, using the operation name the Pentagon has given to US operations against Iran. “Two aircraft were involved in the incident. This was not due to hostile fire or friendly fire.”At least five crew members were aboard the tanker that went down, a US official told CNN.The second aircraft that landed safely was also a KC-135, the official said.The release said more information would become available as “the situation develops” and asked for patience as more details were gathered “to provide clarity for the families of service members.”A KC-135 flight crew typically includes three to four service members, according to the Air Force: a pilot, co-pilot, and boom operator, which is the person who refuels other aircraft mid-air from the KC-135. Mona Hamoudi and Zahra Sarbali of Islamic Republic of Iran react after Alanna Kennedy of Australia scores their teams third goal during the AFC Women's Asian Cup Australia 2026 match at Gold Coast Stadium on March 5, in Gold Coast, Australia.Cameron Spencer/Getty ImagesA fifth member of Iran’s women’s national football team has withdrawn her asylum claim and left Australia for Iran,the latest in a series of reversals involving players who had initially sought refuge during the Women’s Asian Cup tournament.That leaves just two Iranian women still inAustralia on humanitarian visasfollowing a flurry of activity by immigration officials after the team’s exit from the tournament.The women were granted asylum after claiming a fear of persecution if they returned to their war-stricken homeland following theplayers’refusal to sing Iran’s national anthemduring the opening match against South Korea. Exterior of Dubai International Airport after two drones came down in the vicinity of the airport, amid the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on March 11.Stringer/ReutersFlights are temporarily suspended at Dubai International Airport after a fuel tank nearby caught fire during a “drone-related incident” early on Sunday.Dubai’s Civil Aviation Authority announced the temporary suspension “as a precautionary measure to ensure the safety of all passengers and staff,” the Dubai Media Office said.Raj Dholakia told CNN he was at the airport waiting to board a flight home to Toronto, via New York, when authorities evacuated the entire floor covering three gates.“There were hundreds of people – resting, sleeping or walking – everyone was told to go to the nearest staircase and go down,” Dholakia said.“The escalator was full and even lifts were being used,” he added, speaking from the assembly point, where he estimated up to 1,000 passengers had gathered.With seating scarce, some people sat on the floor, Dholakia said. Australia will not be sending a ship to the Strait of Hormuz, following calls from President Donald Trump for US allies to help secure the waterway, the country’s transport minister said Monday.Catherine King told public broadcaster ABC that the country hasn’t been asked to send a ship to the strait, which has been effectively shuttered by Iran since the war began more than two weeks ago.“Well, we’ve been very clear about what our contribution is in relation to requests, and so far, that is to the UAE – obviously providing aircraft to assist with defence, particularly given the number of Australians that are in that area in particular – but we won’t be sending a ship to the Strait of Hormuz,” King told the ABC.“We know how incredibly important that is, but that’s not something that we’ve been asked or that we’re contributing to,” she added.Trump has ramped up pressure on US allies to send ships to the strait, though he has not explicitly asked Australia to help.“It’s only appropriate that people who are the beneficiaries of the strait will help to make sure that nothing bad happens there,” Trump told the Financial Times in a phone interview Sunday, adding that “if there’s no response or if it’s a negative response, I think it will be very bad for the future of NATO.”On Saturday, Trump said in a post to Truth Social he hopes “China, France, Japan, South Korea, the UK, and others” affected by the closure of the strait will send ships to the area.Some context:Australia and the US are formal defense allies and have strengthened ties in recent years with the AUKUS pact, which aims to provide Australia with nuclear-powered attack submarines from the next decade to counter China’s ambitions in the Indo-Pacific region

A fuel tank is on fire near Dubai International Airport after a “drone-related incident,” Dubai Media Office said Monday morning.The fire broke out before 4 a.m. local time and “Civil Defence teams are currently working to bring the fire under control,” said the office in a statement on X.“No injuries have been reported so far,” it said.Iranian drones have repeatedly targeted Dubai’s key transport hub since the war began, with four people injured last week and a concourse damaged in one attack.

President Donald Trump carries an umbrella as he boards Air Force One at Palm Beach International Airport on Sunday in West Palm Beach, Florida.Nathan Howard/Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Sunday warned that NATO faces a “very bad” future if US allies fail to assist in securing the Strait of Hormuz, sending a harsh message to European nations over the strategic waterway.“It’s only appropriate that people who are the beneficiaries of the strait will help to make sure that nothing bad happens there,” Trump toldthe Financial Timesin a phone interview, adding that “if there’s no response or if it’s a negative response, I think it will be very bad for the future of NATO.”The president touted the US’ assistance to Ukraine in its war against Russia, saying, “We didn’t have to help them with Ukraine. … Now we’ll see if they help us. Because I’ve long said that we’ll be there for them but they won’t be there for us.”Asked what type of assistance he is seeking, the president said, “whatever it takes,” including minesweepers.NATO is a European and North Americandefense allianceset up to promote peace and stability and to safeguard the security of its members. It is not meant to aid a nation when a member state starts a war.“We’re always there for NATO,” Trump later reiterated while returning to the White House from Florida aboard Air Force One. “It’d be interesting to see what country wouldn’t help us with a very small endeavor, which is just keeping the strait open.”Trump also suggested in the Financial Times interview that allies could help address threats coming from the Iranian coastline. He said he wants “people who are going to knock out some bad actors that are along the shore,” referring to Iranian forces that have used drones and naval mines in the Gulf.The president repeated his frustration with British Prime Minister Keir Starmer,  over his lack of immediate support for the US-Israeli strikes on Iran.“The UK might be considered the No. 1 ally, the longest serving, etc., and when I asked for them to come, they didn’t want to come,” he said, noting he discussed the issue with Starmer in a call earlier Sunday.“And as soon as we basically wiped out the danger capacity from Iran, they said, ‘Oh, well we’ll send two ships,’ and I said, ‘We need these ships before we win, not after we win.’ I’ve long said that NATO is a one-way street.”This post has been updated with additional information.

A tanker sits anchored as the traffic is down in the Strait of Hormuz in Muscat, Oman, on March 10.Benoit Tessier/ReutersPresident Donald Trump said he could postpone a planned summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he urges Beijing to help address disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the conflict with Iran.“I think China should help too because China gets 90% of its oil from the Straits,” Trump said in an interview withthe Financial Timespublished Sunday, adding that he would prefer to know Beijing’s position before a planned meeting between the two leaders later this month.“We’d like to know before that. French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris, France, on January 6.Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersFrench President Emmanuel Macron spoke with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian calling on him to bring to an end what he described as Iran’s “unacceptable attacks,” carried out directly or through proxies, against countries across the Middle East.After the call, Macron wrote on X that France’s actions in the region are “strictly defensive,” aimed at protecting French interests, regional partners and freedom of navigation, while warning that it would be unacceptable for France to be targeted.“The unchecked escalation we are witnessing is plunging the entire region into chaos, with major consequences today and for the years to come,” Macron said.The comments follow a decision by Paris to significantly increase its military presence in the region. A man holds a fuel pump as he fills his car tank at a gas station in the Manhattan borough of New York, on Saturday.Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesUS gas prices reachedan average of $3.70 a gallon today, according to AAA, a 24% increase since the war in Iran began February 28. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright acknowledged the economic impacts of the conflict but said enduring the“short-term pain”is better than “to have a nuclear armed Iran.”But even if the war ended today, it could take1 to 3 monthsto get the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil travels,operational again, according to Homayoun Falakshahi, lead crude research analyst at Kpler. It will take time to clear the hundreds of ships waiting for safe passage and for major oil producers to fix damaged facilities, ramp up production and get oil moving.The duration of the war is what really matters, CNN’s David Goldmanreported Friday: the longer the war, the higher the prices.Other ways the war in Iran might hit consumer’s wallets:Plane tickets:As oil prices soar,fuel costs for airlines will, too– which means customers might have to stomach higher ticket prices. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby suggested last week the impact of higher jet fuel costs on tickets would“probably start quick.”Travel expertstold CNN Travelcustomers should book their trips whenever they can, and avoid basic economy in times of uncertainty as it has more restrictions on refunds and rebooking.Groceries:Grocery stores – specifically the produce, meat and dairy aisles – areone of the first placesconsumers will see the effects of higher fuel prices, CNN reported last week. With oil prices rising, the cost to transport goods has increased and is poised to continue going up the longer the war continues. The Trump administration Friday night granted atemporary licensefor Iran to sell oil that has been sitting afloat on tankers.That’s a lot of crude: 140 million barrels worth, which is enough to satisfy the entire world’s oil demand for about one-and-a-half days, according to the US Energy Information Administration.The United States has sanctioned Iranian oil on and off for decades, and the Trump administration has blocked sales of the country’s crude since it abandoned the Iran nuclear agreement in 2018.The optics of the temporary, one-month waiver on sanctions could be difficult. The United States is at war with Iran, and the license allows Iran to sell its sanctioned oil to help finance its war against the United States and its allies.But Iran was selling its oil anyway. China is Iran’s biggest customer, and Iran was allowing its tankers through the otherwise blocked Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, global oil prices have surged over the course of the war to around $110 a barrel. The administration is trying to find any lever it can pull to keep oil prices in check while it wages its war – includingdesanctioning hundreds of millions of barrels of Russianoil last week.The sale of Iranian oil probably would have been accomplished anyway – and this way, it can open up the sales to Western countries instead of going exclusively to China. And because of existing sanctions on Iran’s finances, the country may be unable to obtain the oil proceeds, noted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessentin a statement on Friday.“Iran will have difficulty accessing any revenue generated and the United States will continue to maintain maximum pressure on Iran and its ability to access the international financial system,” Bessent said.The move received praise from David Malpass, former World Bank president and Treasury official during Trump’s first term, who called the decision “a strong economic step.”This post has been updated with additional information.

Gas prices have climbed swiftly since the start of the war three weeks ago, fueled by the effective closing of theStrait of Hormuzthat cut off 20% of the world’s oil supply. Prices hit a nationwide average of $3.91 per gallon today, according toAAA, the highest average price for a gallon of regular gas since October 13, 2022.Collectively, the figures are staggering. Drivers have pumped nearly $4.5 billion more into their gas tanks since the US and Israel first attacked Iran, estimated Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, an online price tracker.A household with two cars is spending an average of $20 to $40 a week more on gas than prior to the conflict, De Haan said.“This is money that is not being funneled into the rest of the economy because Americans are leaving it behind at the pump,” he said.It’s unknown when the war – andattacks on the Middle East’s energy hubs– will end. If gas prices top $4 a gallon andremain there for six months, the typical household will spend about $600 more on fuel during that period, said Scott Hoyt, senior director at Moody’s Analytics. In total, its spending will increase by $750 because higher gas prices will cause other items to become more expensive.And the spike will hit lower-income Americans even harder because they tend to spend a larger share of their household budgets on energy, he said.Read more about how rising gas prices are impacting Americanshere.CNN’s Tami Luhby contributed to this report.

Tehran doesn’t believe Trump’s claim that the US is considering “winding down” its military operation, a senior Iranian source has told CNN.“Contrary to Trump’s claims of a reduction in military activity in the region, Iran has no such estimate and concludes that the enemy’s military posture in the region hasn’t changed significantly,” the official said.It comes after US President Donald Trump made the claim in a social media post Friday – and even as officials said thousands more US troops are heading to the region.But the Iranian official dismissed the president’s comments as “Trump’s psychological operations to control the markets,” following continued chaos caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.Oil prices rose further on Friday to $112 a barrel, as the vital waterway supplying 20% of the world’s oil remains largely closed. Goldman Sachs has even suggested that higher prices could last all the way through 2027.“Tehran has concluded that it should not teach Trump a lesson or a temporary response; it should teach him a historical lesson,” the official said.

Shirley Modlin was in meetings all day Thursday searching for costs to cut. Her small manufacturing facility in Powhatan, Virginia, relies on carbide tools made of tungsten to make precise cuts.The chemical element is used in armor-piercing artillery.So carbide tool prices have more than doubled in the past two weeks, Modlin says.Modlin, owner of 3D Design and Manufacturing, said customers won’t tolerate increased prices to cover the rising tool costs.“Now,with gas prices going up, it’s costing me more, eating away at my profit, and it’s making it very, very difficult for me to sustain,” she added.Modlin offers her staff competitive benefits and raises every year to retain and attract new workers. But last year,tariffs rocked the US manufacturing industry, sending the costs of imported raw materials surging – Modlin’s aluminum and steel costs jumped 65%.She wasn’t able to give any raises last year. And on Thursday, facing another round of surging costs, Modlin had to cut an administrator back from full-time to part-time without benefits.“He’s got a house payment; he’s got bills he’s gotta pay. It’s just awful,” Modlin said. “We have to do something. You can only cut so many breakroom supplies.”Modlin was one of four business owners — a clothing store owner, a bread baker, a spot shipper and a factory owner — CNN spoke to about how they plan to deal with surging fuel costs.Read about their plans here.

When a US Air Force fighter crew is forced to eject, particularly over hostile territory, “everyone” in the military operations center overseeing the mission shifts their focus to finding and recovering the crew members as quickly as possible, a retired Air Force C-17 pilot and former Director of the Personnel Recovery Center in Iraq in 2008, told CNN.“People are pushing assets to help provide air cover for their rescue efforts, you have intelligence capabilities that are identifying the location of a potential crash site, and then you have people that are willing to provide strike and fires that are supporting the rescue forces,” said Dr. Ravi Chaudhary, who also served as Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Energy, Installations, and Environment in the Biden administration. “So it is a huge, huge orchestration and mobilization just to ensure that we get our people home.”CNN reported Friday that one of the US crew members from a downed F-15E Strike Eagle fighter jet has been rescued. The status of the second crew member is not clear. F-15s typically carry both a pilot and a weapon systems officer as part of its two-man crew.The crew members go through extensive training for not only how to safely eject, but how to survive once they’ve landed in hostile territory. The two-man crew typically ejects “almost simultaneously,” though it’s not uncommon to be separated from one another based on wind and other factors once they are out of the aircraft and their parachutes have opened.The personnel recovery team “has very, very sophisticated ways” of finding not only the aircraft that has crashed, but the crew, Chaudhary said.For the crew, getting to a safe location immediately and making sure you are “known to rescue forces, either visually or by communications,” is crucial, Chaudhary said. “The critical part is doing that without compromising your position to hostile forces”The training used in these scenarios is called SERE — Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape. The first step, survival, tells the service member to ensure physically they are okay after the landing, check their equipment, and get to a safe location as quickly as possible. The second step, evasion, includes “a number of tactics to lower your profile,” Chaudhary said, and avoid potentially hostile forces or civilians in order to make contact with the rescue team.“I’d be willing to bet that while our first crew member was rescued, nobody’s going home until we get our second crew member,” Chaudhary said. “And to me, that’s the heart of what these men and women do, and they’re doing this at great, great risk.”

Iran’s semi-official news agency posted photos of a drinking water reservoir that officials said was destroyed in a missile strike as well as images of munition fragments that experts told CNN appeared to be from a US-made bomb.CNN could not independently verify that the munitions shown in the image released by the Mehr news agency were found at the site. The photos of the damaged water tank werefirst geolocatedto southern Iran by an independent researcher who posts under the name acceladealer on X and confirmed by CNN.The photo, released by Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency on June 10, 2026, shows the purported remnants of a munition that struck a water reservoir in Southern Iran. Weapons experts who spoke to CNN identified them as being from a GBU-39 series precision-guided munition.MehrThe photo, released by Mehr alongside images of the destroyed water tank in Bamani, Iran, shows components of a GBU-39 series bomb, a precision-guided munition produced in the United States, according to munitions experts Trevor Ball, a former US Army senior explosive ordnance disposal team member, and N.R. Jenzen-Jones, the director of Armament Research Services.Israel and some Gulf states also have the bomb in their arsenals. Ball said the damage to the water tank was broadly consistent with that from a GBU-39.The US launched strikes against Iran on Tuesday in response to Iran downing a US helicopter; it’s unclear if the water tank was hit in those attacks.US Central Command spokesperson Capt. Timothy Hawkins said the command was aware of reports and looking into the situation. He did not answer further questions about the water facility.The caved-in roof of the drinking water reservoir is seen after it was heavily damaged in a strike on June 10, 2026.MehrWater facilities are protected under the Geneva Convention. In March, US President Donald Trump floated the idea of the US attacking Iran’s water desalinization plants in a Truth Social post. The threatraised widespread alarmamong America’s Gulf allies.After the US strikes, MehrquotedAbdul Hamid Hamzehpour, the chief executive of the Hormozgan Water and Wastewater Company, as telling the agency, “Two concrete water-storage reservoirs with a combined capacity of 2,500 cubic meters in the Bamani district were struck by missiles and completely taken out of service.”According to the Iranian Tasnim news agency, which is associated with the country’s Revolutionary Guard Corps, the reservoirs served at least 20,000 Iranians. Commercial vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz on June 30.Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/APOverall traffic through theStrait of Hormuzhas remained “steady” over the past few days but doesn’t appear to be increasing, particularly with regard to the southern Omani route, according to a maritime security authority.The movement of vessels through the crucial waterway via the Omani corridor is “stable” but reports do not indicate a “sustained increase,” the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said Sunday.“Risk remains lower than during the pre-MOU period; however, Iranian intent and capability to conduct intentional hostile action remain, and the environment continues to warrant heightened vigilance despite the absence of recent escalation,” UKMTO said, referring to thememorandum of understandingreached between the US and Iran last month.Meanwhile, the use of a northern Iranian-controlled route also continues, but overall volumes are “difficult to assess” as some ships have turned off their transponders, UKMTO said.Data from shipping intelligence firm Windward also appears to shows traffic through the waterway remaining steady over the past week, with a slight dip on Thursday and Saturday.The existence of competing routes through the channel has only added to theuncertainty facing operators and their crews, even during a tenuous ceasefire in the region.Despite the potential risks, vessels are making the crossing, including via the route which hugs the Omani coastline.Earlier today, aconvoy of at least five vesselstransited the strait via the Omani corridor, one day after several other ships attempted to cross using the same route but U-turned at the last moment.

Women walk past a banner depicting Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in Tehran, Iran on May 6.AFP/Getty ImagesThe structure of Iran’s regime was built following theIslamic Revolution of 1979.This swept away Iran’s monarchy and birthed a state that is part theocracy, part republic, with a handful of semi-democratic institutions swaddled by a system that is ultimately clerical.Here’s a look at how power operates in the country:Supreme leader:Atop Iran’s power structure is the supreme leader — a position currently filled byMojtaba Khamenei. Mourners carry portraits of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, as hundreds of thousands gather to catch a glimpse of the late Iranian leader in a glass coffin in Tehran, Iran in 1989.Christophe Simon and Pascal George/AFP/Getty ImagesAyatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in joint US-Israeli strikes in late February, was Iran’ssecond and longest servingsupreme leader.He became head of state in 1989, after the death of his mentor and predecessor Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.Khomeini, who led the1979 Islamic Revolution, died just under ten years after founding the Islamic Republic.His funeral was recognized byGuinness World Recordsas having the “largest percentage of population to attend a funeral,” with an estimated 10.2 million people — equivalent to one sixth of the country’s population — in attendance, according to official Iranian estimates.The events surrounding the funeral were chaotic, with eight people killed and hundreds injured, according to areport written by the Associated Press news agencyat the time.Iran’s semi-officialIranian Students’ News Agency(ISNA) wrote about the 1989 funeral earlier this week, describing how the enormous crowds exceeded the numbers expected by authorities.Large crowds attend Khomeini's funeral ceremony in 1989.Christophe Simon and Pascal George/AFP/Getty ImagesWhen Khomeini’s coffin began moving in a convoy, mourners surged towards it, causing a crowd crush and forcing the funeral procession to be abandoned, according to ISNA. Mourners hold portraits of Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of his funeral ceremonies in Tehran on Saturday.AFP/Getty Images“Ayatollah,” an Arabic term meaning “sign of God” or “divine sign,” is a senior clerical title in Twelver Shiite Islam typically reserved for scholars who have spent decades studying and teaching Islamic jurisprudence and theology in seminaries.An ayatollah is generally regarded as amujtahid— a jurist qualified to use independent legal reasoning and issue religious rulings.While “ayatollah” is fundamentally a religious title, it has become closely intertwined with political authority in Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, particularly because the country’s supreme leader is expected to have high-level religious credentials. The structure of Iran’s regime was built following theIslamic Revolution of 1979.This swept away Iran’s monarchy and birthed a state that is part theocracy, part republic, with a handful of semi-democratic institutions swaddled by a system that is ultimately clerical.Here’s a look at how power operates in the country:Supreme leader:Atop Iran’s power structure is the supreme leader — a position currently filled byMojtaba Khamenei. The leader is the head of state, commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and has authority over the national police and morality police. He also appoints half of the 12 members of the Guardian Council; Iran’s parliament selects the other half.Guardian Council:This 12-jurist body oversees the activities of Iran’s parliament, determining if laws passed are compatible with sharia and can demand that legislation be revised. The council also approves candidates for parliament, the presidency, and the Assembly of Experts – meaning it can block certain candidates from running for public office.Assembly of Experts:This body of 88 jurists, directly elected by the public from a list of candidates vetted by the Guardian Council, is tasked with checking the authority of the supreme leader. But it is not clear how the assembly exercises its power: it only meets for one week a year; its meetings are secret; and it is not known to have ever challenged a supreme leader’s decisions.President:The head of the elected government is directly answerable to the supreme leader. Eligible for a maximum of two four-year terms, the president implements policies within the framework set out by the supreme leader and spearheads Iran’s diplomacy.Parliament:With 290 members, also elected to four-year terms, the parliament drafts legislation, ratifies treaties and approves the budget. Its sessions are open to the public and its deliberations are broadcast.Security services:The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is an elite military unit tasked with defending the regime, comprising between 150,000 and 190,000 troops, and has an army, navy, air force and intelligence wing. The Basij – a volunteer branch of the IRGC – is responsible for enforcing Islamic morality among the public.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi on Sunday warned of  “appropriate” response after the country accused the US of attacking the Darkhovin nuclear facility in southern Iran.In remarks to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB, Gharibabadi said, “The US attack on the under-construction Darkhovin nuclear power plant constitutes a dangerous assault on Iran’s peaceful infrastructure and places full responsibility for the consequences of escalating insecurity and instability on the United States.”“While strongly condemning this act of aggression, Iran will take appropriate measures to defend its national interests and security,” he added.Earlier Sunday, Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization said theUS struckthe Darkhovin power plant construction site near the Iraqi border.CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment.The UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) earlier on Sunday said it islookinginto reports of an overnight attack on the construction site of an Iranian nuclear power plant.The Darkhovin power plant is in the “very early stages” of construction and the reported attack is unlikely to pose any radiological risk, the watchdog said, but called for “military restraint” in the vicinity of all nuclear sites.

The US military said on Sunday that another service member was killed in action during a controlled detonation of a downed Iranian drone. Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 17.Stringer/ReutersUS Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that about “two-thirds of pre-conflict traffic,” or about 14 million barrels a day, is moving through the Strait of Hormuz despite renewed fighting between the US and Iran.Wright said weekly averages show just under 7 million barrels flow through the Strait of Hormuz a day, and nearly another 7 million more barrels flow through the bypass pipelines.“The ship numbers are down more dramatically (in the Strait of Hormuz), but of course we’re flowing larger tankers now to keep the world markets as well-supplied as we can,” Wright said during an appearance on ABC’s “This Week.”Some key context:Those estimates are “unlikely” if Wright is referring to traffic between July 13 and 19, Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told CNN.Traffic through the strait has slowed since the US and Iran began trading strikes last week. Those strikes effectively ended both countries’ commitment to a14-point agreementthat was supposed to ensure the strait remained open.On Monday, two large crude carriers successfully moved 4 million barrels through the strait, according to Lipow, but another two carriers were badly damaged. Lipow noted that data analytics firm Kpler reported that no tankers have passed through the strait since July 15. Thirty-two ships moved through the waterway on July 10.Lipow has said that about 200 million barrels transited the strait during the first three weeks of the ceasefire agreement.Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates has hired tankers to shuttle oil from inside the strait, which may help oil escape the strait.On the US response to military casualties:Wright was also asked on “This Week” about whether President Donald Trump is planning further retaliation for thekilling of two US service membersin Jordan.“It’s tragic to lose American lives, but this is a mission that will save countless lives going forward,” Wright said. “(Trump’s) focus is on degrading the Iranian ability to terrorize the world, to hold world commerce hostage, as they are doing right now, and to prevent Iran from getting nuclear weapons. That is unchanged.”

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Prime Minister of Iraq Ali al-Zaidi in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on July 14.Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesIraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi is expected to travel to Tehran next week, just days after meeting US President Donald Trump in Washington, in a visit likely to focus on bilateral relations and rising regional tensions.Iraq’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement Sunday that the visit next week will witness “the signing of several memoranda of understanding in areas of common cooperation, to enhance bilateral relations and serve the mutual interests of both countries.”The visit comes at a sensitive time as Baghdad seeks to balance its close ties with Tehran while maintaining its strategic relationship with Washington.Last week, the prime minister saidUS military forceswould leave Iraq by September 30 and that Iran-backed militias would have “no justification” to continue operating after the withdrawal. He made the remarks during a joint appearance with Trump at the White House.Iraq has frequently sought to serve as a bridge between Iran and the United States, using its relationships with both countries to encourage dialogue and help prevent further regional escalation.

People cross the Islamic Revolution Street under a mural depicting a portrait of the late Iranian revolutionary founder Ayatollah Khomeini in downtown Tehran, on Saturday.Vahid Salemi/APFears of a prolonged regional conflict have grown this weekend after the US and Iranlaunched waves of strikesand Washington announced thedeath of two American service membersin Jordan.If you’re just joining us, here’s what to know about the day so far:The US military said it struck a range of Iranian military targets in itslatest round of bombingovernight Saturday into Sunday. The construction site for theDarkhovin Power Plantis near the Iraqi border. He also said Tehran must negotiate if “absolute military victory” is impossible, though he said talks should take place when Iran has “the upper hand.” And Araghchi said he’s yet to meetIran’s new supreme leader.The US carried out anew missile strikeon the outskirts of Abadan, Iran, on Sunday evening local time, according to state media. The city is located in southwestern Iran, near the country’s border with Iraq.Secretary of StateMarco Rubio met with Lebanese President Joseph Aounin Washington on Sunday to discuss a recent agreement between Israel, the US and Lebanon.CNN’s Aileen Graef, Adam Pourahmadi, Catherine Nicholls, Tim Lister, Issy Ronald, Jomana Karadsheh, Eugenia Yosef, Ibrahim Dahman and Sophie Tanno contributed to this report.

US Air Force tanker aircrafts are lined up at Ben Gurion International airport in Lod, near Tel Aviv in Israel, February 24, 2026.Yossi Zeliger/Reuters/FileSenior Israeli officials again warned Sunday that the country will respond to any Iranian attacks as this latest phase of the war continues to escalate.“If Iran attacks Israel, Israel will respond and strike back without any dependence or conditions,” said the country’s defense minister, Israel Katz.Similarly, the Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Lt. Secretary of State Marco Rubio shakes hands with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the State Department, on July 19.State DepartmentUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in Washington, DC, on Sunday to discuss a recent agreement between the US, Israel and Lebanon.﻿During the meeting, Rubio reaffirmed the US commitment to helping implement thetrilateral framework reached in Washingtonlast month, in which Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from two areas in southern Lebanon, paving the way for further negotiations.“The Secretary commended the courage of the Government of Lebanon, under President Aoun’s leadership, for their determined effort to reclaim Lebanon’s sovereignty, disarm Hizballah and dismantle its terrorist infrastructure, and move towards peace,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.A Lebanese statement about the meeting said Aoun also stressed the need to implement the framework, “beginning with securing the first Israeli withdrawal from the first model area.” The agreementdesignated “pilot zones”where Israeli forces can begin transitioning control of territory to the Lebanese military.Aoun’s office said in a previous statement that a Lebanese-US summitwill be held at the White Housethis week.Some background:Before renewed fighting broke out between the US and Iran, amemorandum of understandingsigned by Washington and Tehran had aimed to end the fighting in Lebanon as part of a wider ceasefire plan.Despite that initial agreement — and US-brokered ceasefires between the Israeli and Lebanese governments — fightingbetween Israel and the Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollahhas continued.This post has been updated with a statement from Lebanon.﻿CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq, Oren Liebermann, Sean Lyngaas and Charbel Mallo contributed to this report.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrives to meet his Iraqi counterpart Fouad Hussein in Baghdad, Iraq, on June 28.Hadi Mizban/APIranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says he’s yet to meet Iran’s new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamanei since he was appointed back in March.In a wide-ranging interview, Araghchi also said the security shortcomings that allowed Israel to strike Iran’s leadership at the outset of the war still exist.Here are some of the key points of his conversation with podcaster Javad Mogouyee:• Before the war:Speaking about negotiations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in February, Araghchi said: “I told Witkoff, ‘Have you ever attended a meeting where there was a possibility of being bombed at any moment?’”• US-Israeli strikes:Araghchi said the bombing of the leadership compound in Tehran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and much of his family in February “was carried out through a security vulnerability, and this security vulnerability still exists.”• When he learned of Khamenei’s death:The foreign minister said that “from the very first day,” plans were in place to close the Strait of Hormuz if the leader was targeted. “I immediately contacted the foreign ministries of the region and said: We will strike US military bases; understand that this action is against America,” he added.• On meeting the new supreme leader:“I still have not met Agha (leader) Mojtaba in person during this period of the leader’s tenure. Only a very small number of people have met with him.”• Military readiness:“During the eight months between the two wars (June 2025 and February 2026), Iran’s launcher system was changed in such a way that no matter how much we fired, our missiles would not run out,” Araghchi claimed.• During the conflict:“I and the deputy foreign ministers did not leave the foreign ministry building. For several hours a day, we would drive around the city in a vehicle; I could not put my mobile phone aside.”• Next steps:“If we do not have the ability to achieve an absolute military victory, we must negotiate. Negotiations should take place when you have the upper hand on the military front.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy meets with Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine in Kyiv on July 20.Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout/ReutersIran has condemned theattack by Ukraine on an Iranian vesselin the Caspian Sea, the route for much of the country’s trade with Russia.Three crew members were injured and one seafarer killed aboard the ship, according to regional governor Hadi Hagh-Shenas on Sunday.The vessel had been carrying a cargo of iron and was sailing from Astrakhan to Anzali, “a safe and reliable corridor for commercial exchanges between the two ports,” Hagh-Shenas said.Ukraine launched long-range drone attacks on vessels in the Caspian on Saturday.The attacks were “a sign of the continuation of the irrational and hostile approach of the Ukrainian regime” toward Iran, the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.“Responsibility for the consequences arising from the adventurism of the head of the Ukrainian regime will rest with that regime and its supporters and instigators,” the ministry said.Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires was summoned to the foreign ministry following the attack.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X Monday that he raised the incident in calls with European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, warning that the action “cannot go unanswered.”Some background:Ukraine said Saturday it had struck ships in the Caspian Sea that were transporting military goods from Iran to Russia.Ukraine had “achieved very good results from long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X.“Specifically, these include ships that were involved in transporting military cargo from Iran, as well as a warship,” Zelensky said.Iranian officials have said that the United States has also recently attacked facilities on the Caspian Sea. Vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on June 3.Stringer/Reuters/FileAswe reported earlier, the deputy foreign ministers of Iran and Oman held talks in Tehran about the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.The vital waterway was effectively been closed by Iran since the US and Israel began the war back in February.It is the main route for shipping crude from oil-rich countries such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to the rest of the world.Both Tehran and Muscat have Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) in the strait.According to the United Nations, a state has“sovereign rights”to explore, exploit, conserve and manage the natural resources of the waters in its EEZ.However, under theUnited Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea(UNCLOS), “ships of all States, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea.”A coastal state should not “hamper the innocent passage of foreign ships through the territorial sea,” it says, except in specific outlined scenarios. It may “take the necessary steps in its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent,” UNCLOS outlines.

US President Donald Trump speaks at the White House on July 24.Eric Lee/Getty ImagesAs President Donald Trump pleads for tens of billions of dollarsto pay forthe nation’s war with Iran, Democrats in Congress have offered an unequivocal — and historically unusual — message.No.Trump’s operation in Iran has now become the most partisan war in modern US history, marking the first time that one party is willing to fully reject wartime funding requests from the country’s commander-in-chief.Democrats are, for the first time in at least a century, in lockstep against a war from the start. They are refusing to support more funding. They are voting en masse to demand Trump pull troops out. They are even rejecting a broader Pentagon policy measure in protest — which includes provisions mostly unrelated to this particular war, such as one that would raise troop pay.It’s a seismic political shift from years past, when Democrats would cower from accusations of not supporting troops in the middle of a conflict. But party lawmakers contend that the American public, including Republican voters, are on their side, and that the GOP’s support for the war will be a real dividing line heading into the November election.GOP leaders are furious, with Speaker Mike Johnson calling it “shameful” for Democrats to refuse funding for the Pentagon, especially amid concerns about depleted munitions and as the administration has sought nearly $70 billion more in emergency cash to help pay for military operations in Iran.Democrats’ opposition is multifold. The party is generally more skeptical now of foreign entanglements and much less sympathetic to Israel, the key US partner in Iran. But the party is even more suspicious of Trump — particularly compared to the last GOP administration in wartime — and are incensed at how he’s handled nearly every part of the war in Iran.Readmore hereon how Trump’s operation in Iran has now become the most partisan war in modern US history.

A man pumps fuel into his vehicle at a petrol station in Tehran, Iran, on March 26.Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesAmid high inflation and widespread damage to infrastructure, the Iranian government has warned that heavily subsidized petrol prices may have to be raised.The issue is a sensitive one among Iranians. When the government raised fuel prices by 50% in 2019, nationwide protests quickly escalated into broader anti-government unrest and were met with a sweeping security crackdown and an internet blackout.A change in petrol prices or fuel rationing is certain, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Saturday, according to Iranian state television.“We certainly need strategies for managing gasoline consumption because, as we know, the government is naturally subsidizing the price at which gasoline is sold to the public,” she said.“It is obvious that a solution must be adopted to balance gasoline consumption … As for whether it will involve changes to the quota or to the price, the public will certainly be informed carefully, transparently, clearly, and honestly,” Mohajerani added.Petrol is sold in Iran using three different tiers. Last December, the government introduced a higher rate for drivers consuming more than 160 litres (42 gallons) of petrol per month.The head of Iran’s state fuel distribution company also warned of shortages in an interview on Sunday.If high fuel consumption continues and production and import constraints persist due to damage to facilities, “it may become necessary to adopt measures aimed at maintaining the stability of fuel supply and the country’s energy security,” said Mohammad Sadegh Azimifar, CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution company.Speaking to the news outlet Khabaronline, Azimifar acknowledged the sensitivity of the issue.“The government will not catch people by surprise over petrol. If any decision is to be made, it will first be announced publicly, public opinion will be taken into account, and only then will implementation take place.”

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei speaks at a weekly press conference in Tehran, Iran, July 13, 2026.Shadati/Xinhua News Agency/Getty ImagesThe deputy foreign ministers of Iran and Oman held talks in Tehran about the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a Telegram post Sunday.“During these meetings, the two sides exchanged views on shared principles and operational mechanisms for managing the safe passage of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while respecting the sovereign rights of the two coastal states,” Esmaeil Baghaei said.He said the talks were constructive and that progress had been made.Therehas been no change of status of maritime traffic through Strait of Hormuz, he said, adding that the Omani delegation has left and technical and political consultations between the two sides are continuing.

From left, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif pose after signing a trilateral defense agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia on Friday.Saudi Press Agency/APThe Iran-backed Houthi rebel group claimed today that ittargeted Saudi Arabian forcesin the Yemeni city of Mocha and separately mountedan attack on a major Saudi oil refineryon the Red Sea coast.Notably, these reported attacks come just days after Pakistan and Turkey signed aNATO-style mutual defense pactwith Saudi Arabia in Mecca.The pact stipulates that an attack on any of the three countries “shall be regarded as attack on them all.”The official rationale for the agreement is “to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression” and further provide “for the enhancement of all aspects of defense cooperation among the three states,” according to a statement released by all three countries.Turkey has the second-largest military in NATO, behind only the US, while Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation.Iranian officials have warned since Friday that the mutual defense pactwill not guarantee Saudi Arabia’s security, attempting to downplay the agreement.“The Saudis should understand that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as decades of one-sided dependence on the Americans failed to do so,” Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on Friday.CNN’s Sophia Saifi, Issy Ronald and Abbas Al Lawati contributed to this reporting.

Mohsen Rezaei attends a farewell ceremony for the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in July.Mohammed Salem/Reuters/FileA reshuffle of Iran’s military leadership by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei reflects the political strength of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regime’s hardline stance on negotiations with the US, experts say.Khamenei on Monday made IRGC veteran Mohsen Rezaei the country’s national security chief alongside six other appointments to senior military positions.Rezaei belongs to a faction of the IRGC that believes “the only way to get concessions from the US is the continuation of fighting, exerting pressure on the US and a steady dose of pain on (US President) Donald Trump,” said Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East Politics at George Washington University.His new position shows the increasing power of the IRGC and feeds into the overall Iranian strategy of prolonging the conflict and ensuring that Trump’s allies face defeat in the midterm elections, Azodi said.Saeid Golkar, an associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, said the appointments could also be an effort by Khamenei to install allies in influential positions in case growing economic pressures prompt another public uprising in Iran.Khamenei has not been seen in public since becoming leader following the killing of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the war.Golkar said most of the other six appointees have a background in intelligence, underlining Iran’s increasing reliance on security and intelligence rather than military operations. “The picture we are seeing is the Islamic Republic moving toward a security-dominated bureaucratic regime,” he said.One of the other appointees is Hossein Taeb, a former intelligence chief and “very close ally” of Khamenei, who will now head the Basij, an Iranian volunteer paramilitary militia under the IRGC. As the Trump team’s diplomatic endeavors on both Iran and Gaza continue to flash “Sell” — another of its Middle East peace initiatives appears to have hit the rocks as well.After several rounds of talks between Israel and Lebanon, which began in April, an Israeli official tells CNN there are no dates in the diary for further meetings.The talks are being mediated by the United States and have led to a withdrawal by Israeli forces from small pockets of Lebanese territory, creating what were termed “pilot zones” — to be controlled by Lebanon’s armed forces and kept free from Hezbollah militants.The latest round of talks, which were held last week in Rome, were somewhat overshadowed by an increase in Israeli airstrikes on targets in southern Lebanon, after an explosion killed two Israeli soldiers conducting clearance operations on suspected Hezbollah infrastructure. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, August 7.Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersPresident Donald Trump applied a new condition on talks with Iran, saying he would now require compensation from the country for past misdeeds after Tehran over the weekend said US compensation would be required to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.The back-and-forth suggested the two sides were no closer to reaching an agreement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Yalda Moaiery speaks during the International Women's Media Foundation's Courage in Journalism Awards on October 30, 2023 in New York City.Bonnie Biess/Getty ImagesAn Iranian photojournalist has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for allegedly acting in the interests of Israel and the United States after authorities searched her home and seized electronic devices, according to a US-based human rights group.The announcement comes as rights groups warn of an escalating clampdown on media outlets and journalists in Iran.On Sunday, Yalda Moaiery, a well-known photojournalist who has documented social and political events across Iran throughout her career, announced her sentence on social media: “I got my sentence! 15 years in prison!”Moaieryspoke to CNN in Marchfrom inside Iran, describing the struggles in the country amid US-Israeli strikes and an internet crackdown from Iranian authorities.The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) said Monday that Moaiery’s hearing was held in her absence last month at Tehran’s Revolutionary Court. Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, left, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, center, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif pose after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on Friday.Saudi Press Agency/ReutersPakistan’s Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar has shared “key aspects” of the NATO-stylemutual defense pactbetween Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi.In a Monday call, Dar explained the recently signed agreement’s “objectives of strengthening strategic cooperation and contributing to regional peace and security,” according to Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.Araghchi thanked Dar for “sharing the key aspects of the agreement,” the ministry posted on X.Iranian authorities did not immediately comment on the call.What is the defense agreement?The three nations have signed a mutual defense pact that stipulates an attack against any of them “shall be regarded as an attack against them all.”The agreement between the three US allies, which wassigned in Mecca on Friday, comes as Saudi Arabia faces threats on multiple fronts, and compels each country to intervene if another is attacked.Iranian reaction showed dissatisfaction toward the agreement, with a senior Iranian official warning it would not guarantee Saudi Arabia’s security. Tehran has demanded theUS lifts its naval blockadeof Iranian ports before it reopens the Strait of Hormuz, among several conditionsCurrently, the US blockade order applies to all Iranian ports, both inside and outside the strait — but what does a blockade entail?A blockade is a tool of economic warfare as much as it is kinetic warfare.The Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare defines a blockade as “the capture of contraband, and the capture or destruction of enemy property found at sea.”“These methods deny an enemy the chance of economic revenue from its exports and the benefits of imports that support its war effort,” the manual says.To be legal, the imposition of a blockade must follow certain rules, including:It must be declared and notified, meaning warnings must go out to ships that it might affect.It must be effective, meaning the US must have the ships and aircraft to enforce it.It must be impartial, affecting the vessels of any nation.It cannot be targeted solely at civilian populations, but harm to civilians is acceptable.It must not block access to neutral ports and may not block a strait, like Hormuz, which Trump has said is open to international shipping unrelated to Iran.

US President Donald Trump holds up a memorandum that re-instates sanctions on Iran after he announced his decision to withdraw the United States from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal in the Diplomatic Room at the White House on May 8, 2018.Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesThe US-Iran war is now in its sixth month, with President Donald Trump saying yesterday that the US is“low-keying” negotiationswith Tehran.Direct talks with Iran appear to have faltered, with a previously agreed upon ceasefire now in tatters.The Trump administration’s tense relationship with Tehran started in his first term:InMay 2018, Trump announced he waswithdrawing the USfrom the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, previously negotiated by President Barack Obama. Trump said he viewed the deal as “one-sided.”InApril 2019,the US formally designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Tehran’s most powerful military institution, as aforeign terrorist organization. The move marked the first time the US designated a part of another government as a terror group. Iran responded by declaring the US a “state sponsor of terrorism.”Iran announced inJune 2019that it would ramp up enrichment of low-grade uranium after the US imposed several rounds of sanctions, originally lifted under the Iran nuclear deal.InJanuary 2020, Trump ordered an airstrike in Iraq to kill Iran’s top general, Qasem Soleimani – a move that previous US presidents had considered far too provocative. Thousands of people flooded the streets of Iran to mourn Soleimani.Iran vowed retaliation, ultimately firing missiles at Iraqi bases that housed American troops a few days later. No lives were lost, andTrump respondedby promising more sanctions. As tensions ran high, Iranmistakenly shot downa Ukrainian passenger jet, attributing it to a fear of US aggression. All 176 people on board were killed.

Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Monday.Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesTraffic through theStrait of Hormuzhas remained “subdued” over the past week and “weakened further into the weekend,” maritime intelligence firm Kpler said Monday, even as Iran and Oman signal an agreement on navigation through the key waterway could be within reach.Confirmed crossings fell from 15 on Friday to 11 on Saturday and six on Sunday, Kpler said. Around half of these journeys used the Iranian-approved northern route, while the route of 10 vessels could not be determined.Tehran recently issued alist of demandsfor the US to fulfill before Iran reopens the vital chokepoint, through which one-fifth of global crude oil typically flows. The demands included an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, withdrawing military forces from Iran’s vicinity and permanently ending the war.Meanwhile, traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, another critical maritime trade route, is “considerably more active, recording 116 crossings over the same period,” Kpler posted on X.Daily traffic is relatively stable there, with 43, 37 and 36 vessels traversing the waterway over the three-day period, Kpler said, despite growing concerns over the Iran-backed Houthi group’s targeting of shipping in the region.

Members of Houthi security force stand guard at a rally in Sanaa, Yemen, on July 17.Khaled Abdullah/ReutersTensions escalated this weekend between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia,as we’ve been reporting.Both the Houthis and the internationally recognized Yemeni government released statements on the exchange of attacks, notably both calling themselves the “Yemeni Armed Forces.”Here’s a closer look at the Houthis and how they got to where they are:Who are the Houthis?The Houthi movement, also known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), is one side of the Yemeni civil war. It emerged in the 1990s, when its leader, Hussein al-Houthi, launched “Believing Youth,” a religious revival movement for a centuries-old subsect of Shia Islam called Zaidism.The Zaidis ruled Yemen for centuries but were marginalized under the Sunni regime that came to power after the 1962 civil war. Al-Houthi’s movement was founded to represent Zaidis and resist radical Sunnism, particularly Wahhabi ideas from Saudi Arabia. His closest followers became known as Houthis.Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when Houthi forces stormed the capital Sanaa and toppled the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict spiraled into a wider war in 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to beat back the Houthis.Nowadays, Sanaa is still under Houthi control, alongside much of the west of the country.Who are they allied with?The Houthis are backed by Iran, which began increasing its aid to the group in 2014 as the civil war escalated and as its rivalry with Saudi Arabia intensified. Iran has provided the group with weapons and technology for, among other things, sea mines, ballistic and cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a 2021reportfrom the Center for Strategic and International Studies.The Houthis form part of Iran’s so-called “Axis of Resistance” - an anti-Israel and anti-Western alliance of regional militias backed by the Islamic Republic.

When Mohsen Rezaei entered the room, everyone fell silent. I interviewed the former commander who was then military advisor to Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, at a secret location in Tehran in early June.Rezaei never raised his voice, spoke softly, even when conveying hardline positions. Speaking of possible renewed US-Israeli attacks against Iran, he bluntly threatened to expand the war beyond the Gulf Region.“We will give another dimension to the war by attacking these other American bases,” he said in a calm tone. He also warned the US against a ground assault of Iran, saying “then the world will understand Iran’s true capabilities, because our land power is many times greater than our missiles.”Rezaei talks about military confrontation with a superpower like the US with the calm of someone who has witnessed combat firsthand and believes in Iran’s military power and perseverance. That seems to be one of the reasons Iran’s Supreme Leader appointed him as the head of the Islamic Republic’s Supreme National Security Council.“Considering your valuable experience, I am hereby appointing you, one of the first commanders in the triumphant 8-Year Sacred Defense, to be my representative to the Supreme National Security Council,” a post on X attributed to the Supreme Leader said.Rezaei has been described as a hardline pragmatist, and that certainly showed in our interview. While demanding the immediate release of $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets to unblock a deadlocked negotiations process with the Trump administration, he also said Iran was willing to turn a page with the US if a larger peace deal is reached.“This can be a new horizon for the future of Iran and America. President Donald Trump said yesterday the US is“low-keying” negotiations with Iran, signaling an emphasis on increasing economic pressure on the country.Trump is the latest American president to come up against a hardline Iranian regime, with the conflict now in its sixth month.Here’s a look at how some of Trump’s predecessors interacted with Tehran:President Jimmy CarterPresident Carter announces at the White House, on April 7 1980, that he has broken diplomatic relations with the government of Iran because of the "illegal and outrageous holding" of 50 US hostages in Tehran.Bettmann Archive/Getty ImagesAlmost two years after becoming president, Carter faced the Iran hostage crisis after 90 people, including 66 Americans, were taken hostage when the US embassy in Tehran was seized following theIranian Revolution.At the beginning of the crisis, Carter sent US officials to Iran to negotiate the release of the hostages, though Iran’s then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khomeini refused to meet with them.Carter’s foreign policy team “often seemed weak and vacillating” during the crisis, according to theUS Office of the Historian.A week later, Carter ordered Iranian assets in US banks to be frozen. In April 1980, when only some of the hostages had been released, Carter cut diplomatic ties with Iran, announcing further sanctions and ordering all Iranian diplomats to leave the US.The crisis was eventually resolved after US officials, via Algeria, were able to negotiate the release of the hostages.On January 19, 1981, the US and Iran signed an agreement to release them, and to unfreeze Iranian assets. After more than a year in captivity andminutesafter Carter left the presidency, the hostages were released.President Ronald ReaganUS President Ronald Reagan is seen here giving a speech on the Iran Contra affair in the Oval Office at the White House in 1987.Shepard Sherbell/Corbis/Getty ImagesCarter’s successor Ronald Reagan declared Iran a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1984. But in 1986, his administration began covertly looking into ways to improve its relationship with Tehran, despite backing Iraq in the Iran-Iraq war.Reagan approved a high-profit sale of weapons to Iran despite an embargo, in the hopes that it would yield the return of Americans held hostage in Lebanon by Hezbollah, a militia with close ties to Iran. Funds from some of the arms sales were diverted to the Contras, a minority Nicaraguan political group that was fighting the leftist Sandinista government.The scandal was called theIran-Contra affair, and it broke just before the 1986 midterm elections, posing an enormous threat to Reagan and his party.According to PBS, when the scandal emerged, Reagan publicly denied that any operation had taken place. He then retracted his statement a week later, saying that it had not been an arms-for-hostages deal.“Despite the fact that Reagan defended the actions by virtue of their good intentions, his honesty was doubted,” PBS explains. “Polls showed that only 14 percent of Americans believed the president when he said he had not traded arms for hostages.”President Barack ObamaUS President Barack Obama speaks with President Hassan Rouhani of Iran during a phone call in the Oval Office on September 27, 2013.Pete Souza/White House/Getty ImagesObama managed to negotiate a tentative rapprochement with Tehran during his tenure, having vowed tounfreeze US-Iran relationsin his 2008 presidential campaign.Obamaspoke by telephonewith Iranian President Hassan Rouhani in 2013, the first direct conversation between leaders in Washington and Tehran since 1979, when Carter talked by telephone with Shah Mohammed Reza Pahlavi before Pahlavi was overthrown.Also in 2013, after years of negotiations, alandmark agreementwas reached that slowed Iran’s nuclear development program in exchange for the lifting of some sanctions that caused the country’s economy to stagnate.The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), finalized two years later in 2015, capped Iran’s uranium enrichment for 15 years and facilitated UN-led inspections to ensure Tehran’s adherence to the deal, in exchange for partially dissolving sanctions on Iranian oil wealth and unfreezing billions of dollars in assets.Trump withdrew fromthe deal in his first term.

Smoke rises during Houthi strikes on the Red Sea port city of Mocha, Yemen, on Sunday.ReutersThe United Nations’ special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, has said that he is “deeply concerned” by recent Houthi attacks on the Yemeni city of Mocha.Yesterday, Yemen’s government armed forces said they’d“thwarted a treacherous terrorist attack by the Houthi militia,”hours after the Iran-backed militant groupclaimed it had carried out an attackon Saudi forces in Mocha.The Houthis claimed they used “a large number of ballistic missiles and drones” in their attack on the city.Recent Houthi attacks have “put civilians at grave risk” in areas across Yemen, Grundberg said, adding that the “escalation must stop, and civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected.”“These attacks come amid the most significant intensification of military activity since the 2022 UN-brokered truce, sharply increasing the risk of a return to full-scale conflict in Yemen,” Grundberg said in apost on X.The special envoy called on “the parties to exercise maximum restraint” and to work with his office to “de-escalate and prevent the further erosion of what the truce achieved for Yemeni civilians.”“This conflict can only end sustainably through an inclusive political process, and escalation is taking Yemen in the opposite direction,” he said.

First aid responders and residents search the site of an Israeli airstrike in Deir al-Zahrani, Lebanon on Saturday.Abbas Fakih/AFP/Getty ImagesThree Israeli soldiers were seriously injured in a Hezbollah attack in southern Lebanon early Saturday morning, according to the Prime Minister’s office.The attack prompted a wave ofdeadly Israeli strikesin southern Lebanon that killed at least 11 people, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry, including women and children.In a rare Saturday statement, the Israeli Prime Minister’s office accused Hezbollah of violatingthe ceasefireby attacking the Israeli soldiers.The Israel Defense Forces said it struck a headquarters of Hezbollah’s elite Radwan force in response, killing what they described as a battalion commander and several others. Flames and smoke rise from the port of Mocha during a strike in Yemen, on Friday.Abdulnasser Alseddik/APUS President Donald Trump said yesterday that he would“never apologize” for taking military action against Iran, arguing that higher gas prices have been worth it in his pursuit of preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon.This comes as Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said earlier today that Tehran hasnot decided whether to resume negotiationswith the US.Here’s the latest on the conflict in the Middle East:Israel launched a series of airstrikes in southern Lebanon today, killing at least nine people, according to Lebanon’s state-owned National News Agency (NNA), in thedeadliest day since the June ceasefire.Separately, one person was killed and eight injured after the Iran-backed Houthi militia grouplaunched six ballistic missiles at Yemen’s port of Mochaon the Red Sea last night, according to Yemen’s Armed Forces.An “unknown projectile”crashed into the hull of a bulk carrierin the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre said, adding that the crew was reported safe.Shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz in the past seven days was17% of the pre-conflict average, according to the UKMTO.CNN’s Kit Maher, Aida Karimi, Mitchell McCluskey, Sophie Tanno, Eyad Kourdi, Laura Sharman and Charbel Mallo contributed to this reporting.

Houthi supporters shout slogans during an anti-Saudi rally amid an escalation with the kingdom, in Sanaa, Yemen, July 31.Khaled Abdullah/ReutersThe Iran-backed Houthi militia grouplaunched six ballistic missilesat the Yemeni city of Mocha last night, killing one person, according to Yemen’s Armed Forces.This was the latest attack on Mocha since the conflict in Yemen escalated last week, with the Houthis claiming to be targeting Saudi forces inside the country.Here’s what to know about the group:Who they areThe Houthi movement, also known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), is one side of the Yemeni civil war. It emerged in the 1990s, when its leader, Hussein al-Houthi, launched “Believing Youth,” a religious revival movement for a centuries-old subsect of Shia Islam called Zaidism.The Zaidis ruled Yemen for centuries but were marginalized under the Sunni regime that came to power after the 1962 civil war. Al-Houthi’s movement was founded to represent Zaidis and resist radical Sunnism, particularly Wahhabi ideas from Saudi Arabia. His closest followers became known as Houthis.Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when Houthi forces stormed the capital Sanaa and toppled the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict spiraled into a wider war in 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to beat back the Houthis.Nowadays, Sanaa is still under Houthi control, alongside much of the west of the country.Houthis’ alliesThe Houthis are backed by Iran, which began increasing its aid to the group in 2014 as the civil war escalated and as its rivalry with Saudi Arabia intensified. Iran has provided the group with weapons and technology for, among other things, sea mines, ballistic and cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a 2021reportfrom the Center for Strategic and International Studies.The Houthis form part of Iran’s so-called “Axis of Resistance” - an anti-Israel and anti-Western alliance of regional militias backed by the Islamic Republic.How powerful is the group?American officials have been tracking iterative improvements in the range, accuracy and lethality of the Houthis’ domestically produced missiles. Initially, home-grown Houthi weapons were largely assembled with Iranian components smuggled into Yemen in pieces, an official familiar with US intelligence told CNN previously.They have previously used drones and anti-ship missiles to target commercial ships – some of which aren’t believed to be linked to Israel – prompting the USS Carney, a warship in the Red Sea, to respond to distress calls.

The kingdom has facedincreasing attacksfrom the Houthis, who also declared a blockade on the al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea on July 20.

The armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government said a short while ago that it has carried out181 attacks on the Iran-backed Houthi rebelsin the past 24 hours, claiming that dozens of Houthi militants had been killed or wounded.Both the Yemeni government and the Houthis have reported clashes and drone strikes in recent weeks, as tensions between the twohave ramped up.Here’s a closer look at the Houthis:Who are the Houthis?The Houthi movement, also known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God), is one side of the Yemeni civil war. It emerged in the 1990s, when its leader, Hussein al-Houthi, launched “Believing Youth,” a religious revival movement for a centuries-old subsect of Shia Islam called Zaidism.The Zaidis ruled Yemen for centuries but were marginalized under the Sunni regime that came to power after the 1962 civil war. Al-Houthi’s movement was founded to represent Zaidis and resist radical Sunnism, particularly Wahhabi ideas from Saudi Arabia. His closest followers became known as Houthis.Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when Houthi forces stormed the capital Sanaa and toppled the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict spiraled into a wider war in 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to beat back the Houthis.Nowadays, Sanaa is still under Houthi control, alongside much of the west of the country.Who are they allied with?The Houthis are backed by Iran, which began increasing its aid to the group in 2014 as the civil war escalated and as its rivalry with Saudi Arabia intensified. Iran has provided the group with weapons and technology for, among other things, sea mines, ballistic and cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a 2021reportfrom the Center for Strategic and International Studies.The Houthis form part of Iran’s so-called “Axis of Resistance” - an anti-Israel and anti-Western alliance of regional militias backed by the Islamic Republic.How powerful is the group?American officials have been tracking iterative improvements in the range, accuracy and lethality of the Houthis’ domestically produced missiles. Initially, home-grown Houthi weapons were largely assembled with Iranian components smuggled into Yemen in pieces, an official familiar with US intelligence told CNN previously.They have previously used drones and anti-ship missiles to target commercial ships – some of which aren’t believed to be linked to Israel – prompting the USS Carney, a warship in the Red Sea, to respond to distress calls.CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman and Tim Lister contributed to this reporting.

Majid Abdullah Al-Nuzaili.Al-Nuzaili claimed that dozens of Houthi militants had been killed or wounded.CNN is unable to verify many of the claims made by either side, but the conflict has flared up in recent weeks after the Houthis declared a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.Saudi Arabia is the main backer of Yemeni government forces.Both the government and the Houthis have reported clashes and drone strikes along many parts of the frontlines, which stretch several hundred miles from the Red Sea coast to Yemen’s border with Oman.Analysts say the Houthis appear to be mobilizing for an offensive that would aim to take more of the Red Sea coastline.

It is getting harder to estimate the volume of shipping using the key Strait of Hormuz, as more vessels pass through with trackers off and ship-to-ship transfers disguise the amount of oil reaching global markets, analysts say.Traffic through the waterway remains low and although Iran and Oman are negotiating over the waterway, there are no immediate signs of a deal.The number of ships known to be transiting the Strait of Hormuz varies from a couple to about a dozen on a daily basis. Not all are tankers; many operators are still deterred from using the strait because of sporadic Iranian drone attacks.Thirteen vessels transited on Thursday, according to maritime intelligence group Windward, with four of those inbound and nine outbound. Of the outbound traffic, four vessels — including a tanker laden with 2 million barrels of Saudi crude - sailed with their satellite trackers off.On Friday, shipping data showed no visible crude-oil tanker transits.That same day, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that between 8 and 9 million barrels a day were getting through Hormuz on a running average. We used to sell oil, but now we cannot sell it,” he said.

US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House, on August 10.Jacquelyn Martin/AP/FileUS President Donald Trump claimed on Friday that he plans todeclare the Strait of Hormuz a US territoryafter “we finish defeating Iran,” prompting Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi to say that the waterway “cannot be seized with a tweet, an aircraft carrier, an executive order, or a campaign speech.”The Strait of Hormuz has been at the centre of frequent clashes between Tehran and Washington since the start of the war itself.The two sides signed amemorandum of understandingin June, where they agreed to pause fighting while they negotiated a lasting end to the conflict, but this broke down following a series of disputes related to the waterway.Here’s a look back at how fighting resumed last month:July 1:US and Iranian negotiators travel to Doha, Qatar, for indirect negotiations. Vice President JD Vance discusses anti-fraud initiatives during a visit to Wisconsin Air National Guard's 128th Air Refueling Wing at Milwaukee Mitchell Airport in Milwaukee on July 8.Jim Vondruska/ReutersOne of the Trump administration’s biggest problems in extracting itself from the Iran war is the list of very absolutist goals that President Donald Trump and his team laid out.Thegoalshave included complete Iranian surrender, regime change, Iran never getting a nuclear weapon and ending Tehran’s support for its Middle East proxy groups like Hezbollah.As the war — now in its sixth month — has dragged on, this list of goals has conspicuously shifted and been pared back.
