Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu votes in Likud party primary elections in Jerusalem, on Monday.Ohad Zwigenberg/ReutersPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told US envoy Jared Kushner that Israel would not withdraw any of its forces in Gaza or allow reconstruction to begin until the complete disarmament of Hamas, according to a senior Israeli official.The two also agreed that an American general would oversee the decommissioning of Hamas weaponry, the official said, which would be the first step in the demilitarization of the shattered enclave.Hamas has refused to disarm unless it is sequenced with an end to near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza and the beginning of a withdrawal of Israeli forces currently occupying more than half of the territory.Board of Peace director Nickolay Mladenov and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair alsotook partin the meeting. US President Donald Trump makes a speech at the David Mack Center for Training and Intelligence, on Friday.Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOn Friday, President Donald Trump saidhe plans to declarethe Strait of Hormuz a US territory after “we finish defeating Iran,” which he said would happen “pretty soon.”Days before, the president claimed the US had “total control” over the waterway. “We own it, and at some point, maybe they’ll do something, and then they get blown away,” Trump told reporters.Trump has repeatedly claimed the US “owns” the Strait of Hormuz, parts of which form the territorial seas of Iran and Oman. There are important constitutional requirements that must be cleared first,” Jason Chuah, Professor of Maritime Law at City, University of London and Distinguished Fellow, Maritime Institute of Malaysia, told CNN.“Under international law, annexation is contrary to the United Nations Charter. Territories including bodies of water can only be taken through agreement or cession,” Chuah added.While the occupation of a territory might give the occupying state control over the area, he said, “on its own, it does not convey legal title.”Simon Baughen, Professor of Shipping Law at Swansea University, said the path toward claiming Hormuz as a US territory was unlikely to come to fruition.“Under international law, this could only be done if Iran agreed to cede its territorial waters in the strait to the US,” he said. “I think this is a very unlikely scenario.”A more likely outcome, Baughen suggested, could be that the US, Iran and Oman agree to open the Strait of Hormuz and charge tolls to vessels passing through the waterway.But, he said: “That is also illegal under customary international law and also the provisions of the 1982 UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea) Treaty.”Neither Iran nor Oman has absolute rights over the Strait of Hormuz, Chuah pointed out. “Freedom of navigation prevails. That is the law,” he said.“The Strait is neither Iranian property nor Omani property in the ordinary sense of a piece of real estate. It is sovereign territory very much subject to an international regime of maritime navigation,” he said.“A navy can control a waterway. US President Donald Trump reiterated today “the number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon,”as we’ve reported.He is the latest American president to come up against a hardline Iranian regime, with the war now in its sixth month.Here’s a look at how some of Trump’s predecessors interacted with Tehran:President Jimmy CarterPresident Carter announces that he has broken diplomatic relations with the government of Iran because of the "illegal and outrageous holding" of 50 US hostages in Tehran, at the White House in Washington D.C., April 7, 1980.Bettmann Archive/Getty ImagesAlmost two years after becoming president, Carter faced the Iran hostage crisis after 90 people, including 66 Americans, were taken hostage when the US embassy in Tehran was seized following theIranian Revolution.At the beginning of the crisis, Carter sent US officials to Iran to negotiate the release of the hostages, though Iran’s then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khomeini refused to meet with them.Carter’s foreign policy team “often seemed weak and vacillating” during the crisis, according to theUS Office of the Historian.A week later, Carter ordered Iranian assets in US banks to be frozen. In April 1980, when only some of the hostages had been released, Carter cut diplomatic ties with Iran, announcing further sanctions and ordering all Iranian diplomats to leave the US.The crisis was eventually resolved after US officials, via Algeria, were able to negotiate the release of the hostages.On January 19, 1981, the US and Iran signed an agreement to release them, and to unfreeze Iranian assets. After more than a year in captivity andminutesafter Carter left the presidency, the hostages were released.President Ronald ReaganUS President Ronald Reagan is here giving the Iran Contra speech in the Oval Office at the White House in 1987.Shepard Sherbell/Corbis/Getty ImagesCarter’s successor Ronald Reagan declared Iran a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1984. He then retracted his statement a week later, saying that it had not been an arms-for-hostages deal.“Despite the fact that Reagan defended the actions by virtue of their good intentions, his honesty was doubted,” PBS explains. “Polls showed that only 14 percent of Americans believed the president when he said he had not traded arms for hostages.”President Barack ObamaUS President Barack Obama speaks with President Hassan Rouhani of Iran during a phone call in the Oval Office September 27, 2013.Pete Souza/White House/Getty ImagesObama managed to negotiate a tentative rapprochement with Tehran during his tenure, having vowed tounfreeze US-Iran relationsin his 2008 presidential campaign.Obamaspoke by telephonewith Iranian President Hassan Rouhani in 2013, the first direct conversation between leaders in Washington and Tehran since 1979, when Carter talked by telephone with Shah Mohammed Reza Pahlavi before Pahlavi was overthrown.Also in 2013, after years of negotiations, alandmark agreementwas reached that slowed Iran’s nuclear development program in exchange for the lifting of some sanctions that caused the country’s economy to stagnate.The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), finalized two years later in 2015, capped Iran’s uranium enrichment for 15 years and facilitated UN-led inspections to ensure Tehran’s adherence to the deal, in exchange for partially dissolving sanctions on Iranian oil wealth and unfreezing billions of dollars in assets.Trump withdrew fromthe deal in his first term.

Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf attends a meeting in Switzerland in June.Urs Flueeler/Pool/ReutersIranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf accused the US of trying to force more concessions from Iran.“Americans think squeezing Iran harder will win concessions that were never part of the agreement,” Ghalibaf, who is Iran’s top negotiator,wrote Tuesday in a poston X.The official also said that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are “way out of their league.”“Stop waiting for the clown crew to pull a rabbit out of their hat and clean up the mess you made,” Ghalibaf said.Last week, Bessent said the US wouldapply measuresto Iran that have “never been seen.” US President Donald Trump has alsoindicatedthat he plans to apply more economic pressure on Tehran.

Air defense forces in the United Arab Emirates detected two ballistic missiles launched toward the country from Iran on Tuesday, with one falling outside UAE territorial waters and the second landing within its territorial waters, the UAE Defense Ministry said.In a statement, the ministry said the country’s armed forces were fully prepared to respond to any threats and would “resolutely confront anything that targets the destabilization of the state’s security.”The statement did not mention casualties, damage or interception efforts.“The Ministry of Defense confirms that it is fully prepared and ready to deal with any threats,” the statement said, adding that the UAE would continue to protect its sovereignty, security, stability and national interests.Earlier Tuesday, the UAE’s National Emergency Crisis and Disaster Management Authority said on X that air defense forces had detected a “missile threat” targeting the country and urged residents to “remain in a safe place and follow warnings and updates from official sources.”

Qatar voiced support Tuesday for ongoing efforts between Oman and Iran to reach an agreement over the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump’sthreatto attack Oman if it interferes with US operations in the strategic waterway.Majed al-Ansari, a Foreign Ministry spokesman and adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said Doha hopes that an agreement between Muscat and Tehran would help create the conditions for renewed diplomacy amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict.“A ceasefire, guaranteeing freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, and a return to the negotiating table represent the only way forward,” al-Ansari said during the Foreign Ministry’s weekly press briefing.He said Qatar remains focused on containing the crisis and returning the parties to negotiations, citing developments in the Strait of Hormuz and what he described as a violation of a previous ceasefire.Trump on Monday threatened military actionagainst Omanif it obstructed US efforts in the Strait of Hormuz.“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News’ Trey Yingst.Al-Ansari said there were no new developments in talks between Oman and Iran. But diplomatic efforts are still underway to reach an arrangement that could pave the way for renewed negotiations and help prevent further escalation in the region, he said.

A view of the Namakabrud township in Chalus county in Mazandaran province, north of Tehran, on September 5, 2025.Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty Images/FileIran could face gas supply shortages in several provinces this winter following damage to the country’s natural gas infrastructure during theUS-Iran war.Houshang Seydali, director of gas distribution coordination at the National Iranian Gas Company, warned that “without strong, coherent and coordinated plans, several provinces could experience gas-supply problems,” according to Iran’s state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA).He said three northern provinces, North Khorasan, Mazandaran and Golestan, “could face more difficult conditions,” while restrictions could be imposed on eight other provinces depending on pressure levels and conditions across the gas network.Seydali urged households and industry to conserve energy, saying gas demand management would be critical during the winter months, IRNA reported.He also warned that electricity generation could be affected because “a significant portion of Iran’s electricity generation depends on natural gas.”“Industry, households and National Iranian Gas Company employees will all need to contribute,” Seydali said. Reducing consumption during periods of extreme cold would help maintain supplies for both homes and industry, he added.IRNA noted thatattackson Iran’s gas infrastructure during the ongoing US-Iran war have reduced the country’s gas production capacity.

A drone view shows vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, in June.Stringer/ReutersIran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf todayreiterated his country’s key demandsof the US for reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz, including the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and the US ending its military threats.The Strait of Hormuz has been at the center of frequent clashes between Tehran and Washington since the start of the war in late February.In June, the two sides signed amemorandum of understandingin which they agreed to pause fighting while they negotiated a lasting end to the conflict. But this broke down following a series of disputes related to the waterway.Here’s a look back at how fighting resumed last month:July 1:US and Iranian negotiators traveled to Doha, Qatar, for indirect negotiations. The delegationsmade “positive progress,”Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said.July 7:Iranfired on three commercial vesselsin Oman’s territorial waters near the Strait of Hormuz, according to a US official. US Central Command said itlaunched strikes against Iranas“punishment.”July 8:Iran warned it woulddeliver a “crushing response”to the US strikes, and the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched attacks at85 US military targetsacross Bahrain and Kuwait. US President Donald Trump castigated Iran’s leaders as “evil, sick people” at the NATO summit in Turkey, saying the memorandum of understandingwas “over.”Hours later, the USlaunched more strikesagainst Iran.July 9:Tehran said the US militarystruck a railway bridgein northern Iran. CENTCOM said the US hitaround 90 military targetsin another round of strikes. A US official told CNN that both countries werecontinuing to engage in technical negotiationson nuclear issues.July 10:Trump said the US hadagreed to continue talkswith Iran, but also that Washington had informed Tehran the ceasefire was no longer in effect. Ghalibaf said Tehran was prepared for“all-out defense”if the US broke the agreement. The Trump administrationimposed fresh sanctionson Tehran.July 11:Iran’s foreign minister accused the US ofviolating a clauseon Tehran’s nuclear program in their agreement.July 12:The IRGC announced it hadclosed the Strait of Hormuzafter firing a warning shot at a vessel attempting to use an unauthorized route to cross the waterway. The US militarylaunched more strikeson Iran and insisted that thestrait was still open.July 13:US attacks across Irancontinued into the afternoon,killing at least two people, Iranian media reported. Trump said he wouldreinstate a blockadeof Iranian ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and the US carried outmore strikeson Iran overnight.CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq, Hira Humayan, Pamela Brown, Lex Harvey, Zachery Cohen, Jessie Yeung, Kevin Liptak, David Winkie, Isaac Yee, Clay Voytek, Betsy Klein, Aida Karimi, Lauren Kent, Jennifer Hansler, Rhea Mogul, Dalia Abdelwahab, Aleena Fayaz, Izzy Lippolis, Aileen Graef and Piper Hudspeth Blackburn contributed to this post.

The al-Mirani Fort and traditional houses are surrounded by mountains, amid the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Muscat, Oman, on March 12, 2026.Benoit Tessier/ReutersPresident Donald Trump’s suggestionhe will bomb Omanif it impedes US efforts in the Strait of Hormuz is “not a credible threat in any sense,” according to Jasmine el-Gamal, former Middle East adviser at the US Department of Defense.Speaking to CNN’s “Connect the World” on the possible reasons for Trump’s warning, el-Gamal told Christina Macfarlane the conflict has been going on close to “six months now with no seeming end in sight and so, understandably, the president is frustrated.”Citing the president’s previous comments on erasing civilization in Iran and earlier attempts to caution Oman, she added: “He’s prone to these kinds of bombastic statements when he’s feeling frustrated.”His comments come after a 60-day deadline for US-Iran talks expired Monday, ending the window for the two countries to negotiate the terms of a final deal to end the war and settle issues such as Tehran’s nuclear program.

President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One, on Sunday, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APPresident Donald Trump said Tuesday that there are no talks underway or scheduled with Iran, one day after saying his administration had established a back channel with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the military arm that reports to the country’s supreme leader.“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect. The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.Just one day prior, Trump said his administration had established a back channel with the IRGC. “They’re good poker players, but they’re dying,” Trump told Fox News. “I have no time schedule. I’m not in a hurry.”Iran’s IRGC denied that any back-channel talks with the United States were taking place.Trump’s Tuesday comments also sharply differ from an assessment offered by special envoy Jared Kushner to Fox News on Monday.“I will say that the conversations between the US Government and different areas of the Iranian government at all areas is probably more robust than it’s maybe ever been,” he said, adding that the Trump administration is “having very positive and active conversations.”Last week, the president said US forces had completed mine-sweeping operations to clear naval mines from the waterway, a claim he reiterated Tuesday. He’s also repeatedly claimed that the strait is open, despite lagging shipping traffic and Iran asserting otherwise.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf presides as lawmakers chant in support of the IRGC while wearing military uniforms in Tehran on February 1.Hamed Malekpour/Wana News Agency/ReutersIran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has been a key negotiator with the US during the conflict.As we reported earlier, he is also set to lead a“high level parliamentary delegation” to Iraqtomorrow, according to Iranian state media.There, officials from both countries will discuss “strengthening bilateral relations, border security, counterterrorism efforts, expanding economic cooperation, and advancing the implementation of agreements between the two countries,” Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported.Ghalibaf alsoissued a list of demands todaythat he said the US needed to meet before Iran reopens the Strait of Hormuz.The demands include the US lifting sanctions on Iranian oil and ending military threats, both of which were part of theMemorandum of Understandingagreed upon by Tehran and Washington back in June.Who is he?Ghalibaf, who has led Iran in negotiations with the US, is a regime insider with areputation for suppressing dissent.As a teenager, he joined the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s, and later commanded the IRGC’s air force.Ghalibaf was involved in crushing pro-reform student protests in 1999. He oversaw the suppression of further student demonstrations in 2003 as police chief and held a senior security role during the widespread protests that followed Iran’s disputed 2009 election.He was also the mayor of Tehran for 12 years, during which he modernized the capital’s infrastructure and oversaw ambitious housing programs as well as the creation of green spaces.

US President Donald Trump posted an image on social media today showing the Strait of Hormuzlabeled as “New US Territory.”This comes after Trump said Friday thathe plans to declarethe strait a US territory after “we finish defeating Iran.”Trump has repeatedly claimed the US “owns” the Strait of Hormuz, parts of which are in the territorial waters of Iran and Oman. However, maritime law experts point out claiming a territory is not this simple.“Under US law, claiming territory by a presidential declaration (or) decree is not enough. There are important constitutional requirements that must be cleared first,” said Jason Chuah, professor of maritime law at City St. George’s, University of London, and a distinguished fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia.“Under international law, annexation is contrary to the United Nations Charter. Territories including bodies of water can only be taken through agreement or cession,” Chuah told CNN.While the occupation of a territory might give the occupying state control over the area, he said, “on its own, it does not convey legal title.”Simon Baughen, professor of shipping law at Swansea University, said the path toward claiming Hormuz as a US territory was unlikely to come to fruition.“Under international law, this could only be done if Iran agreed to cede its territorial waters in the strait to the US,” he said. “I think this is a very unlikely scenario.”A more likely outcome, Baughen suggested, could be that the US, Iran and Oman agree to open the Strait of Hormuz and charge tolls to vessels passing through the waterway.But, he said: “That is also illegal under customary international law and also the provisions of the 1982 UNCLOS(United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea)Treaty.”Neither Iran nor Oman has absolute rights over the Strait of Hormuz, Chuah pointed out. “Freedom of navigation prevails. That is the law,” he said.“The strait is neither Iranian property nor Omani property in the ordinary sense of a piece of real estate. It is sovereign territory very much subject to an international regime of maritime navigation,” he said.“A navy can control a waterway. It cannot, merely by controlling it, rewrite the law of title,” Chuah added.

The United States has criticized Israeli strikes on a Syrian airbase early on Tuesday.“We are deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Airbase constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability,” said the Trump administration envoy on Syria, Tom Barrack.He added that ​Washington was ⁠encouraging all parties ⁠to ‌prioritize “logical discourse” over further ‌military ‌incidents.Israel has not confirmed it carried out the strikes on the air base, which is near Idlib in north-western Syria and has few serviceable aircraft.Barrack said on X that the government in Damascus had neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces. “It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel.”The Syrian Foreign Ministry described the strikes as “an unjustified aggression, a blatant violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region.”It said Israel was seeking to “drag the region toward further tension and instability.”Barrack has mediated direct talks between Syria and Israel in an effort to make sure that an uneasy truce is sustained, especially in southern Syria where Israeli forces continue to occupy strategic heights on Syrian soil.The two sides have yet to reach agreement on a more lasting peace settlement.US President Donald Trump has praised Syia’s leader Ahmad al Sharaa, who led an uprising that ousted long-time president Bashar al Assad 18m months ago.

US President Donald Trump posted an image on social media Tuesday showing the Strait of Hormuz labeled as “New US Territory.”The picture of a map includes a circle around the strategic waterway, which is located between Iran and Oman at the entrance to the Persian Gulf, with the words “New US Territory” displayed over the area.The president’s Truth Socialpostcame one day after he said declaring the strait a US territory was a “great idea.”“I mean we control it,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked what he meant last week when he said he would soon declare the strait to be US territory.“We control it with the blockade, and I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” the president added.The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a key bargaining chip in the war with Iran. The strategically vital strait has been effectively closed by Iran since fighting began in late February, disrupting a major route for global oil shipments.Expertshave saidneither side has full control of the waterway.

enrichment” related to Iran’s “nuclear needs.”CNN’s Billy Stockwell, Alayna Treene, Kevin Liptak and Mostafa Salem contributed to this reporting.
